worst_places.quote: By ROI and dependencies: (1) CI on affected with a correct base — changes the pipeline-time asymptotics and requires nothing; (2) the production set in namedInputs — amplifies both the local cache and the freshly enabled affected CI; (3) boundaries warn→error — stops the *growth* of architectural debt (cheap to start, long to burn down — hence early); (4) the Nx upgrade one major per PR — unlocks modern mechanisms and de-risks every following step; (5) the buildable forest — the most labour-intensive with the least effect, dismantled as touched.
worst_places.problem: 85 words in one sentence carrying five ranked items, each with its own em-dash justification, plus three unexpanded abbreviations (ROI, CI, PR) and two rare words ('asymptotics', 'labour-intensive'). The RU original is already an over-limit 74 words; the EN expansion pushes it past any phone screen. This is the answer to the highest-value question of the capstone chapter, so it is exactly the sentence a reader will re-read.
worst_places.before: By ROI and dependencies: (1) CI on affected with a correct base — changes the pipeline-time asymptotics and requires nothing; (2) the production set in namedInputs — amplifies both the local cache and the freshly enabled affected CI; (3) boundaries warn→error — stops the *growth* of architectural debt (cheap to start, long to burn down — hence early); (4) the Nx upgrade one major per PR — unlocks modern mechanisms and de-risks every following step; (5) the buildable forest — the most labour-intensive with the least effect, dismantled as touched.
worst_places.after:
Order them by payoff and by what depends on what.

1. Move CI (continuous integration) to `affected` with a correct base. It changes how pipeline time grows with the repo, and it needs no other fix first.
2. Add the `production` set to namedInputs. It makes both the local cache and the affected CI you just enabled hit far more often.
3. Switch boundaries from warn to error. It stops architectural debt from *growing* — cheap to start, slow to pay off, so start early.
4. Upgrade Nx one major per PR (pull request). Each step unlocks modern mechanisms and makes the next step safer.
5. Dismantle the buildable-lib forest last. It costs the most work for the least effect; convert libs as you touch them.

The principle: first what is cheap and changes the slope of the curve, then what is expensive and removes a whole level.

worst_places.before: For every package an instance satisfying the requirements is chosen (typically the highest compatible one offered). `singleton` forces a single instance even on conflict (warning + the already-loaded one wins); `strictVersion` upgrades the conflict from a warning to an error; `eager` puts the dependency into the initial bundle, removing the async load (and creating the async-boundary requirement for consumers — chapter 11).
worst_places.after:
For each package the runtime picks one instance that satisfies every declared range — usually the highest compatible version on offer. The three flags change that outcome:

- `singleton` forces one instance even when the versions conflict. You get a warning, and the copy that loaded first wins.
- `strictVersion` turns that conflict from a warning into an error.
- `eager` puts the dependency into the initial bundle, so it is not loaded asynchronously. In exchange, every consumer now needs an async boundary — see chapter 11.

patterns: THE dominant pattern: the English version is systematically harder than the Russian one, in every single file of the zone. Over-limit sentences, ru → en: ch08 10.4% → 23.6%; ch09 6.1% → 21.8%; ch10 8.5% → 19.3%; ch11 6.6% → 23.2%; ch12 10.4% → 27.6%; ch13 10.3% → 32.2%; ch14 5.3% → 15.1%. The cause is mechanical and repeatable: Russian joins facts with a dash or a colon and drops the copula, and the translation keeps that single-sentence shape while adding ~19% more words plus English's obligatory articles, auxiliaries and 'that'-clauses. A borderline 28-word RU sentence lands at 40-50 words in EN. Nothing about the technical content needs to change — the fix is a per-file pass that splits every dash-joined RU clause chain into separate EN sentences. Chapter 13 is the worst case (a third of all sentences over limit) and chapters 12 and 11 are close behind.

Second pattern: acronyms are treated as ambient vocabulary rather than as terms that need a first use. `CI` is used 8-26 times per chapter and is never expanded once in any of the 15 chapters of the course, so the 'explained in the chapter that introduces it' allowance does not apply — it is never introduced at all. The same holds for `MF`, `PR`, `CDN`, `README`, `HMR`, `CORS`, `SSR`, `SEO`, `e2e`. `MF` is worse than merely bare: it is overloaded, meaning «микрофронтенды» in chapters 09 and 14 and 'Module Federation' in chapters 10 and 11 — and in chapter 09 it carries both meanings within a single file. A one-time pass that expands each acronym at its earliest occurrence in the course, plus a decision to write 'Module Federation' in full and reserve MF for microfrontends, fixes all 14 files.

Third pattern (structural, and mostly a strength worth codifying): every chapter uses the same reliable skeleton — Theory → 'В рабочем монорепо' (five runnable grep/nx commands for someone else's repo) → 'Что добавляем в проект' → exercise with explicit **Вход:** prerequisite → worked solution → Check yourself → Common mistake framed as 'a developer from the single-app world'. Rubric C and E scores are high (4.3 each) precisely because of this skeleton: the **Вход:** line means a reader returning after a week always knows what state the workspace is in, and the 'Common mistake' section reliably names the wrong mental model before correcting it. The one place the skeleton leaks is theory density: the 'Ответы на edge cases' and 'Разбор решения' blocks routinely run 5-16 consecutive paragraphs with no diagram or code between them (ch09 en: 16 paragraphs / 532 words; ch13 en: 8 paragraphs / 495 words; ch12 en: 12 paragraphs / 535 words), which is where the D score of 3.5 comes from.
notes:
Microfrontends overlap: chapters 09-11 COMPLEMENT the `microfrontends` topic rather than duplicate it, with one contradiction to resolve. The topic teaches MF generically and polyrepo-flavoured (hand-written ModuleFederationPlugin configs, iframes, web components, single-spa, style isolation, cross-MFE state, interview answers); the course teaches the same negotiation mechanics strictly through Nx generators and adds material the topic does not have at all — Nx auto-sharing every workspace lib as an unversioned singleton, and the resulting first-wins skew across independently deployed remotes. Overlap is confined to remoteEntry/container, the bootstrap async boundary, singleton/strictVersion/eager, and the two-reacts dispatcher story. Send a reader who wants concepts or interview answers to the topic; send anyone building or auditing a real Nx federation to the course, which is markedly better written (the topic came out systemic-refactor with 40-90-word fact sandwiches). Two things to fix at the seam: the topic frames `strictVersion: true` as a staging/CI-only diagnostic, while course ch11 prescribes it permanently in production for react/router/state libs — pick one; and the two use different abbreviations for the same idea (topic: MFE, expanded once; course: MF, never expanded), with no cross-link in either direction.
Chapter 14 delivers as the practical payoff. It is a real procedure, not a summary: a layer → source-of-truth → what-to-look-for table, seven numbered steps each with a copy-pasteable command, a catalogue of eight archaeological finds with diagnosis and treatment, a 10-question deliverable, a worked reference run against mini-shop, 🔴/🟡/🟢 triage, and an explicit one-fix-per-PR discipline plus a 'don't open the epic cleanup PR' warning. A middle developer could execute it on a real repo in the promised hour or two. Its problems are purely linguistic: CI appears 26 times unexpanded, and the ROI-ordering answer — the single most valuable paragraph in the chapter — is one 74-word (RU) / 85-word (EN) sentence.
